title: Dyspnea -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Dyspnea is a subjective respiratory sensation characterized by insufficient air intake arising from complex physiologic, psychological, social, and environmental interactions. Acute presentations occur in pulmonary embolism, asthma exacerbation, pneumonia, or heart failure, whereas chronic manifestations develop in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease, obesity, or neuromuscular weakness. The symptom may appear as air hunger, chest constriction, tachypnea, or increased respiratory effort, often restricting activity and diminishing functional capacity. Dyspnea is a clinical manifestation rather than a discrete disease entity.

title: Dyspnea -- Introduction
content: Dyspnea, commonly described as shortness of breath, is a subjective sensation of uncomfortable or difficult breathing arising from diverse medical, environmental, psychological, and physiological factors. Patients frequently report chest tightness, air hunger, rapid breathing, or a sensation of insufficient air. Dyspnea affects millions worldwide and may serve as the primary manifestation of respiratory, cardiac, neuromuscular, systemic, or psychogenic disorders, or a combination thereof. Psychosocial, cultural, and physiologic factors, including anxiety, depression, hormonal status, obesity, and overall fitness level, influence the perception and severity of dyspnea. Clinically, acute dyspnea develops over hours to days, subacute dyspnea evolves over several days up to 4 weeks, and chronic dyspnea persists for more than 4 weeks. [1] [2] [3]

title: Dyspnea -- Etiology
content: Dyspnea, whether acute or chronic, is a symptom of an underlying condition rather than a distinct disease. The etiologies may be broadly classified into 6 primary categories: respiratory, cardiac, neuromuscular, psychogenic, systemic, or multifactorial.

title: Dyspnea -- Etiology
content: Acute dyspnea is most commonly due to either pulmonary or cardiovascular causes. Respiratory causes can be further categorized as diseases of the upper airway, chest wall, diaphragm, or lung parenchyma. Such organization allows clinicians to prioritize potentially life-threatening conditions and streamline evaluation. title: Dyspnea -- Epidemiology
content: Dyspnea is a common reason for emergency department visits, representing roughly 5% of cases each year. The leading causes include lower respiratory tract infection, heart failure, COPD, and asthma, which together account for the majority of presentations. The relative frequency of these conditions varies with patient age and comorbidities. [7]

title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Neurophysiological Mechanisms of Dyspnea
content: The severity and presentation of dyspnea can vary independently of measurable physiologic changes, arising from complex interactions among central and peripheral neural pathways. The symptom reflects the integration of afferent signals from chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors with motor command signals within the central nervous system. Both the automatic (brainstem-mediated) and voluntary (cortical) components of the respiratory motor system contribute to the perception and modulation of breathing effort.

title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Neurophysiological Mechanisms of Dyspnea
content: Mechanoreceptors in the airways, lungs, and chest wall provide continuous sensory feedback to respiratory centers regarding lung volume and airway status. Three primary types of pulmonary mechanoreceptors are involved: slow-adapting stretch receptors, rapidly adapting or irritant receptors, and juxtacapillary (J) receptors.

title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Neurophysiological Mechanisms of Dyspnea
content: Slow-adapting stretch receptors convey information about lung inflation, helping to regulate tidal volume and inhibit overexpansion (Hering–Breuer reflex). Rapidly adapting receptors respond to changes in lung volume and to chemical or mechanical irritants, such as inhaled particles or inflammatory mediators. C fibers, originating from J-receptors in the alveolar walls near pulmonary capillaries, are activated by both mechanical and chemical stimuli. These afferents travel via the vagus nerve to the brainstem, influencing respiratory rate, depth, and reflexes such as cough.

title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Neurophysiological Mechanisms of Dyspnea
content: Peripheral chemoreceptors, located in the carotid bodies at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries and in the aortic bodies of the aortic arch, primarily monitor arterial oxygen tension. The sensitivity of these receptors increases in hypercapnia and acidosis, augmenting ventilatory drive under hypoxic conditions. Activation triggers afferent impulses via the glossopharyngeal nerve to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla, stimulating excitatory respiratory neurons and increasing ventilation. Carotid bodies contribute approximately 15% of total ventilatory drive under normal conditions and assume a dominant role during hypoxemia.

title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Neurophysiological Mechanisms of Dyspnea
content: Central chemoreceptors exert primary control over baseline respiratory drive. Located on the ventral surface of the medulla and within the retrotrapezoid nucleus, these receptors respond to changes in cerebrospinal fluid pH, which reflects arterial carbon dioxide (CO2) levels. C02 diffuses freely across the blood-brain barrier, forming carbonic acid and lowering cerebrospinal fluid pH, which stimulates ventilation. Increases in pH, reflecting hypocapnia, suppress ventilation. This tightly regulated feedback system maintains stable arterial CO2 and pH levels during changing metabolic demands. title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Neural Integration and the Perception of Dyspnea
content: Respiratory centers in the medulla oblongata and pons generate the basic rhythm of breathing. Integrated sensory input from peripheral chemoreceptors, which monitor oxygenation, and central chemoreceptors, which detect pH and CO2 levels, continuously modulates this rhythm. Additional modulation occurs via cerebellar and cortical structures that integrate volitional and emotional influences, producing a unified neural signal transmitted to the diaphragm, external intercostals, scalene muscles, and accessory respiratory muscles. [11] [12]

title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Neural Integration and the Perception of Dyspnea
content: Dyspnea commonly arises when a mismatch exists between the central respiratory motor command and mechanical or sensory feedback from the lungs, chest wall, or airways. This “afferent–efferent mismatch” occurs when actual mechanical responses, such as airflow obstruction, respiratory muscle weakness, or increased ventilatory demand, fail to meet the perceived need for ventilation. The brain interprets this discrepancy as an uncomfortable awareness of breathing effort, intensifying the sensation of dyspnea.

title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Nonpulmonary Causes of Dyspnea
content: Anemia is a classic nonpulmonary cause of dyspnea. Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity initially triggers increased cardiac output through tachycardia, potentially elevating pulmonary venous pressures and stimulating pulmonary C fibers, contributing to breathlessness. Inadequate oxygen delivery to active skeletal and respiratory muscles can produce local metabolic acidosis, activating muscle metaboreceptors and increasing ventilatory drive. These combined cardiovascular and peripheral mechanisms underlie the sensation of dyspnea in patients with anemia.

title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Nonpulmonary Causes of Dyspnea
content: Similarly, patients with chronic lung disease often develop a sedentary lifestyle. Dyspnea in such individuals may result more from deconditioning than from intrinsic lung disease. Deconditioned muscles rely on anaerobic metabolism even during mild activity, producing lactic acid that stimulates ergoreceptors and increases neural output from respiratory centers, accelerating breathing. The precise contribution of local acidosis and ergoreceptor stimulation to dyspnea remains uncertain. Additionally, patients with chronic inactivity may exhibit heightened sensitivity to dyspneic stimuli, perceiving normal exertion as abnormal.

title: Dyspnea -- Pathophysiology -- Nonpulmonary Causes of Dyspnea
content: Heart failure constitutes a common cardiac cause of dyspnea. Impaired left ventricular function elevates pulmonary venous and capillary pressures, leading to interstitial and alveolar fluid accumulation. Resulting congestion reduces lung compliance, increases the work of breathing, and stimulates J receptors and pulmonary C fibers, which transmit afferent signals via the vagus nerve to the brainstem, producing rapid, shallow breathing and the sensation of air hunger. Reduced cardiac output also limits oxygen delivery to skeletal and respiratory muscles, promoting early anaerobic metabolism, lactic acidosis, and activation of muscle metaboreceptors, further intensifying dyspnea.

title: Dyspnea -- History and Physical
content: Acute dyspnea suggests conditions such as asthma exacerbation, pneumonia, anaphylaxis, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, acute myocardial ischemia, cardiac tamponade, or heart failure. In contrast, chronic or progressive dyspnea is more often due to COPD, interstitial lung disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or cardiac dysfunction. The quality of dyspnea (eg, “air hunger,” “inability to take a deep breath,” or “chest tightness”) provides additional diagnostic clues. Associated features such as orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, wheezing, cough, chest pain, fever, or edema guide differentiation between pulmonary, cardiac, metabolic, or psychogenic causes.

title: Dyspnea -- History and Physical
content: Evidence of respiratory distress on physical examination includes tachypnea, use of accessory muscles, nasal flaring, cyanosis, hypoxia, or altered mental status. Inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation of the chest may reveal asymmetry, dullness to percussion, wheezes, crackles, or decreased breath sounds, suggesting effusion, consolidation, or obstruction. Findings such as jugular venous distension, displaced apical impulse, murmurs, or gallops indicate a cardiogenic process. Peripheral findings such as clubbing, cyanosis, edema, or muscle wasting may indicate chronic hypoxemia or systemic disease. See Table 2 for a summary of characteristic historical and physical findings associated with major etiologic causes of dyspnea.

title: Dyspnea -- History and Physical -- Critical Signs Requiring Immediate Evaluation
content: A heart rate exceeding 120 bpm, respiratory rate above 30/min, pulse oxygen saturation (SpO2) below 90%, use of accessory respiratory muscles, difficulty speaking in full sentences, altered mental status, stridor, asymmetric breath sounds, diffuse crackles, diaphoresis, unstable arrhythmias, and cyanosis are all indicators that urgent evaluation is required. For patients who are unstable at initial presentation, clinicians should perform a rapid assessment and stabilization following the Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol.

title: Dyspnea -- History and Physical -- Critical Signs Requiring Immediate Evaluation
content: During the initial rapid assessment, the clinician should inspect the chest for evidence of trauma, such as open wounds, bruising, or asymmetrical chest movement, and examine the neck for tracheal deviation, which may indicate a tension pneumothorax. Lung auscultation evaluates the presence and symmetry of breath sounds, with absent or diminished sounds on one side suggesting pneumothorax or hemothorax. Palpation of the chest wall can detect crepitus from subcutaneous emphysema or flail segments, while percussion identifies hyperresonance indicative of pneumothorax or dullness consistent with hemothorax. Observation of respiratory rate and accessory muscle use provides a measure of dyspnea severity.

title: Dyspnea -- History and Physical -- Assessment of Hemodynamically Stable Patients
content: For stable patients, a thorough history is essential to guide evaluation and management. Clinicians should obtain a detailed description of events leading to symptom onset, including medication and diet adherence in patients with heart failure, recent allergen exposure or upper respiratory infection in patients with asthma, new food exposures preceding symptoms, vaccination status, and any recent surgery, trauma, or immobilization. Inquiry should also cover exacerbating and relieving factors, as well as changes in symptom severity over time.

title: Dyspnea -- History and Physical -- Assessment of Hemodynamically Stable Patients
content: Past medical history is critical. Clinicians should determine whether the condition is new or recurrent and ask about prior diagnoses such as asthma, CAD, heart failure, deep venous thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism. A history of prior intubation is important, as patients with previous airway interventions may be at increased risk for severe symptoms and require repeat intubation in certain conditions, such as asthma.

content: Respiratory assessment begins with the respiratory rate, which may be slow, normal, or rapid in patients with serious underlying illnesses. content: Breath sounds offer additional diagnostic insight. Inspiratory stridor typically indicates upper airway obstruction above the vocal cords, whereas expiratory or mixed stridor generally indicates obstruction below the vocal cords. Wheezing from bronchoconstriction may occur in asthma, acute decompensated heart failure, anaphylaxis, foreign body aspiration, or tumors. Interalveolar fluid produces crackles, most commonly in pneumonia or acute decompensated heart failure. Conditions that limit airflow, such as severe asthma, COPD, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, or hemothorax, result in decreased breath sounds.

content: The evaluation of dyspnea requires a structured, stepwise approach that integrates patient history, focused physical examination, and selective diagnostic testing. Dyspnea may arise from pulmonary, cardiac, hematologic, neuromuscular, or psychogenic causes. Clinicians must synthesize multiple data points to determine the underlying etiology and guide timely management.

content: History and physical examination findings inform the selection of diagnostic tests. Most patients with acute dyspnea undergo a chest radiograph, ECG, complete blood count with differential, and serum electrolytes, including bicarbonate. title: Dyspnea -- Evaluation -- Initial Diagnostic Evaluation
content: Bedside ultrasound in patients with acute dyspnea assists in evaluating left ventricular function, pericardial effusion, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, cardiac wall motion abnormalities, right heart strain in pulmonary embolism, and proximal deep vein thrombosis (DVT). [18] The BLUE (Bedside Lung Ultrasound in Emergency) protocol, developed by Lichtenstein et al, provides a standardized point-of-care approach to assess patients with acute dyspnea rapidly. The protocol examines 3 specific thoracic zones on each side: the upper BLUE point, the lower BLUE point, and the posterolateral alveolar and pleural syndrome (PLAPS) point. Characteristic ultrasound patterns, or “profiles,” correspond to distinct causes of respiratory distress.

Potential risks of CT include contrast-induced nephropathy, allergic reactions to contrast, and radiation-related malignancy.

title: Dyspnea -- Evaluation -- Further Diagnostic Assessment
content: Pulmonary embolism evaluation combines D-dimer testing with CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA). Patients are first stratified according to the Wells criteria for probability of DVT. Individuals with low probability who meet all 8 Pulmonary Embolism Rule-Out Criteria (PERC) require no further testing. Patients who do not meet these criteria or have intermediate probability undergo D-dimer testing. A D-dimer level below 500 ng/mL indicates a low likelihood of DVT or pulmonary embolism and typically requires no additional evaluation. Levels of 500 ng/mL or higher warrant further imaging, preferably CTPA. Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scanning is utilized when CTPA is unavailable or inconclusive.

title: Dyspnea -- Evaluation -- Further Diagnostic Assessment
content: Additional testing may include measurement of negative inspiratory force to assess patients with suspected neuromuscular disease, such as myasthenia gravis or Guillain-Barré syndrome. Blood and sputum cultures are indicated when infection is presumed to cause dyspnea, for example, in pneumonia or sepsis. Sputum cultures identify the specific pathogen responsible for lower respiratory tract infection, allowing targeted antibiotic therapy. Blood cultures determine whether the infection has entered the bloodstream, which influences disease severity and guides treatment intensity. These tests are particularly valuable when dyspnea is accompanied by fever, productive cough, leukocytosis, or other signs of systemic illness. [20] [21] [22] [23]

title: Dyspnea -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Acute Dyspnea
content: If respiratory failure is imminent, clinicians should maintain a low threshold for endotracheal intubation. When appropriate, high-flow nasal cannula or noninvasive ventilation, such as continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP), may be employed. Contraindications to noninvasive ventilation include coma, cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, gastrointestinal bleeding, cardiac instability, status epilepticus, potential upper airway obstruction, and inability to protect the airway.

title: Dyspnea -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Acute Dyspnea
content: Pneumonia is a frequent cause of dyspnea requiring hospitalization. Tools such as the CURB-65 (confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, respiratory rate ≥30/min, blood pressure with systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure ≤60 mm Hg, and age ≥65) score help determine severity and the need for intensive monitoring. Management includes supplemental oxygen and empiric antibiotics, with blood and sputum cultures—and viral testing when indicated—to guide targeted therapy, especially during outbreaks of pathogens such as influenza, SARS-CoV-2, or MERS-CoV.

title: Dyspnea -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Chronic Dyspnea
content: For patients with COPD, management follows the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) guidelines. Pulmonary rehabilitation benefits patients with persistent symptoms despite optimal therapy. [27] Individuals with chronic hypoxemia, characterized by a maximum resting arterial oxygen tension of 55 mm Hg or a maximum SpO2 of 88%, should receive long-term home oxygen therapy. The Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) guidelines direct asthma treatment and emphasize inhaled bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, leukotriene receptor antagonists, and avoidance of known triggers. [28]

title: Dyspnea -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Chronic Dyspnea
content: Since dyspnea is a subjective experience, patient-reported outcome measures, such as the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), Visual Analog Scale (VAS), modified Borg Scale, and the modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) scale, are essential for clinical assessment. These tools are quick to administer, easy to interpret, and valid across diverse conditions, including COPD, interstitial lung disease, heart failure, and advanced cancer. These assessments enable clinicians to quantify dyspnea severity and distress and to monitor response to therapy over time.

title: Dyspnea -- Prognosis
content: Dyspnea is a symptom rather than a disease, and its prognosis depends entirely on the underlying etiology. Across both emergency and outpatient settings, dyspnea consistently portends increased short- and long-term mortality. Patients presenting with dyspnea to the emergency department have markedly higher admission rates and up to a 5-fold increase in mortality when compared with those presenting with chest pain. Dyspnea independently predicts 1-year mortality in ACS and is associated with a higher risk of atrial fibrillation and myocardial infarction, even in individuals without known cardiopulmonary disease. Patients with dyspnea but no CAD have a 4-fold increased risk of sudden cardiac death compared with asymptomatic individuals and more than twice the risk compared with those who have angina.

title: Dyspnea -- Prognosis
content: Dyspnea is an independent predictor of adverse outcomes among patients with conditions such as acute myocardial infarction or COPD. The degree of breathlessness during daily activities—quantified using validated scales such as the Medical Research Council or modified mMRC dyspnea scale, often supplemented by the 6-minute walk test—correlates strongly with mortality in COPD, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, and even in the general population without diagnosed cardiopulmonary disease.

title: Dyspnea -- Complications
content: Complications associated with dyspnea depend on the underlying cause, severity, and duration of illness. Both physiologic and psychosocial sequelae are common. Potential complications include the following: Respiratory failure Atelectasis and pneumonia Acid-base disturbances Structural lung injury Pulmonary hypertension Heart failure Arrhythmias Pulmonary edema Increased risk of stroke and myocardial infarction Sudden cardiac death Deconditioning and exercise intolerance Respiratory muscle fatigue Cachexia Osteoporosis (particularly in patients on long-term corticosteroids) Anxiety and panic symptoms related to breathlessness Depression and overall reduction in quality of life

title: Dyspnea -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Dyspnea, or shortness of breath, is the subjective sensation of breathing discomfort. This disease manifestation may present acutely or chronically and can result from a wide range of underlying conditions affecting the lungs, heart, blood, or neuromuscular system. Healthcare professionals should emphasize to patients that dyspnea is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and warrants thorough assessment to determine its etiology. Patient education should prioritize recognition of red flag symptoms, including rapidly worsening dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, hemoptysis, or peripheral edema. Patients must be instructed to seek immediate medical care if these features occur, as they may indicate life-threatening conditions such as acute heart failure, pulmonary embolism, or myocardial infarction.

title: Dyspnea -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: For patients with chronic respiratory or cardiac conditions such as asthma, COPD, or heart failure, clinicians must provide education on proper inhaler or medication technique, self-monitoring for signs of exacerbation, and clear criteria for when to contact a healthcare provider. Additionally, clinicians should stress the importance of lifestyle modifications, including smoking cessation, weight management, graded exercise, and adherence to vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID-19), to reduce symptom recurrence and improve prognosis.

title: Dyspnea -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Additional strategies should prioritize reducing the risk of cardiopulmonary disease by promoting smoking cessation, minimizing environmental exposures such as secondhand smoke and occupational irritants, and ensuring strict adherence to prescribed therapy. Routine follow-up visits, early intervention for infections, and prompt management of symptom exacerbations can decrease acute care utilization and prevent complications. Healthcare professionals should also support public health efforts by emphasizing that new or worsening dyspnea, particularly when accompanied by chest pain, presyncope, or cyanosis, requires urgent evaluation. Early identification and treatment of underlying etiologies are essential to reducing morbidity and mortality associated with dyspnea.

title: Dyspnea -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes

Healthcare professionals must recognize dyspnea as a symptom rather than a diagnosis, reflecting a wide variety of underlying conditions.
